en: The Scripture of the Six-Syllable Divine Mantra,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India by Imperial Decree. Oṃ vajradhāna ma.
I shall now explain the efficacy of this six-syllable mantra of Mañjuśrī. If there is anyone who,
wishing to achieve accomplishment, maintains this mantra,
they should either consume milk-rice or eat vegetables.
If one eats fruit or consumes milk,
one should eat this food while bathing three times each day; that is,
the first period begins after the fifth watch of the night.
The period after noon is the second watch;
from after dusk until the first part of the night is the third watch.
During these three watches, one should bathe once each.
Each person must wear one set of pure robes;
therefore, three sets of pure robes are required.
One should recite the mantra until it reaches six hundred thousand repetitions.
This is the initial rite for serving and making offerings to Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, if one wishes to receive and practice the sādhana,
one must first paint an image of Mañjuśrī.
As for the method of painting the image:
take a fine white felt that is free of hair or fibers,
and do not cut or break its warp and woof threads.
The pigments must not use glue;
they should be mixed with fragrant liquid for painting.
As for the image of Mañjuśrī:
Seated in the full lotus posture upon a lotus throne,
his right hand performs the gesture of teaching the Dharma,
while his left hand rests palm-upward within his lap.
The body of the image is in the form of a youth,
golden in color;
a white celestial robe covers it from below the navel upward.
The rest of the body is bare;
the head is adorned with a celestial crown, and the body is embellished with necklaces, armlets,
bracelets, and other various ornaments.
On the left side, an image of Avalokiteśvara is painted;
his body is the color of white silver,
adorned with necklaces and garments as is customary.
Seated upon a lotus flower in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*),
his right hand holds a white fly-whisk (*cāmara*).
To the right, an image of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is depicted.
His body is golden in color;
he is adorned with necklaces and ornaments as usual,
and he likewise sits upon a lotus throne, holding a white fly-whisk in his right hand.
In the sky above Mañjuśrī, on both sides,
create two Śuddhāvāsa devas, each holding a flower garland in their hands.
Within the empty clouds, only the upper half of the body appears,
with hands hanging down holding a flower garland;
this is located to the right of the image of Mañjuśrī.
Depict the mantra-holders with their right knees touching the ground and their hands holding incense burners.
Beneath the lotuses where Mañjuśrī and the others sit, depict ponds of water extending everywhere.
On both sides of the Bodhisattva image,
each is depicted upon a mountain peak.
When the painter first began to paint them, he...
On that very day, he observed the eight precepts,
bathed, and put on clean garments before beginning the painting;
he continued until the painting was complete.
If there is a stūpa containing relics, one should install an image of Mañjuśrī;
located on the western side of the stūpa, the image should face west.
If there is no large stūpa, one should install it using a small stūpa.
In front of the Mañjuśrī image, facing west,
one should arrange various flowers, various foods, fruits, and so forth,
making offerings at the three times of day.
Within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one should burn ghee lamps.
This site of enlightenment must be located in a place of profound stillness,
and only a single person should be permitted to provide service there.
If, while reciting mantras in the maṇḍala, one requires flowers,
incense, or other offerings, one should snap the fingers to summon them without uttering a word; instead,
take aloeswood (agaru) and cut it into pieces two finger-widths long.
Dhūlupa oil, *suhaka* (stacte) incense, and thin [incense] are smokeless *khadira* wood charcoal.
If these are unavailable, substitute with *śiṃśapā* wood.
Furthermore, place agarwood within the aforementioned oil and burn it entirely for one night in a fire of khadira wood charcoal before the image;
this continues until the appearance of the dawn light.
Upon seeing Mañjuśrī, all their aspirations were completely fulfilled,
with the sole exception of matters concerning sexual desire.
Apart from these, all other requests will be granted without fail.
Furthermore, there is a method:
before the image, take sandalwood and cut off a piece two finger-widths long. Return [the remainder].
If one burns offerings day and night,
at that time Mañjuśrī will manifest his body before them and preach the Dharma for their sake;
all physical ailments will be completely healed.
One attains mastery over the bodhisattva stages.
Furthermore, regarding the ritual:
before an image, one should smear the ground with *gomaya* (cow dung).
Scatter various kinds of famous flowers.
The practitioner sits on one side within the consecrated ground and recites the mantra one hundred and eight times.
After one month, one will attain clarity of mind and be able to retain all sutras and śāstras.
Furthermore, as a practice, one should constantly recite according to one's inclination each day without forgetting;
this will certainly cause karmic retribution to be received and also lead to its extinction.
Furthermore, according to another method, if one is able to recite this one hundred and eight times every day,
at the time of death one will behold Mañjuśrī;
whatever one’s heart desires, one shall attain rebirth accordingly.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
Mañjuśrī has briefly explained a small portion of its various efficacies.
In this case, the *Ṣaḍakṣarīvidyāmantra-sūtra* translated by Bodhiruci is also contained within this volume of the Song Canon, alongside the *Ṣaḍakṣarīvidyārāja-sūtra*.
It is not found in the Dazang (the Tripitaka). According to the Kaiyuan lu,
it is contained within a single fascicle and is titled the *Liu zi shenzhou jing* (The Scripture of the Six-Syllable Divine Mantra), translated by Bodhiruci.

The sixth fascicle of the *Cloud-Gathering Dhāraṇī Collection Sūtra*, "The Mantra Methods of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and Five Additional Mantras," including the Six-Syllable Dhāraṇī, is a different translation of the same text as [the corresponding work in] the *Dhāraṇī Saṃgraha Sūtra*.
Upon examination, this very sūtra is it;
there is no other *Ṣaḍakṣarīvidyārājñasūtra* consisting of ten spells translated by Bodhiruci.
Now, having examined that sūtra:
This refers simply to those works within the case whose translators' names were lost and which are now appended to the Liang dynasty catalog;
in the Song edition of the canon, one sees the name of a six-character divine mantra within their titles.
To have indiscriminately included it here alongside these works and recompiled it within this single volume is one error; furthermore,
why have you falsely bestowed upon it the title *Liuzhi* (The Stream of Will)?
Therefore, it has now been removed and stated as follows.
